sweep_summary: Plateau Malagasy (plat1254) is in the catalog as 'lexical' on Howe 2021 (JIPA Illustration). The three title-works with stress in the title are all genuinely about Merina word accent but none could be read first-hand: Rakotofiringa 1982 (Strasbourg thèse d'État on the acoustic correlates of Merina accent, 600 pp., French) exists only in print (SUDOC 051222485/078388198/040953521, Harvard Widener Library offsite) — low priority since Howe 2017/2021 digest its findings (pitch the most consistent correlate); Raoniarisoa 1990 (Bangor PhD, Merina) has an open 9.87 MB PDF on Bangor Pure that is could not be reached by automated download (archive.org offline, EThOS blocked, CORE has no text) — abstract read: it argues that 'accent in Malagasy is determined by intonation', which refines the domain note but not the placement facts; HIGH priority to download by browser; Downing '200x' 'Accent in African languages' is the 2010 De Gruyter survey chapter (doi 10.1515/9783110198966.1.381, paywalled), but its 2004 ZASPiL precursor is held by the project and its Malagasy section (p.112, from Beaujard 1998 and Keenan & Polinsky 1998) states penult default, lexically conditioned antepenult on -tra/-ka/-ña/-na, lexical/morphological final stress and alternating secondary stress — confirms the classification. new_statements.relation_note: Same placement facts as Downing 2004 (penult default; antepenult on -tra/-ka/-na finals; final stress in some /e/-final roots and by morphology; leftward alternating secondary stress) and adds the analysis: the antepenult class is underlyingly consonant-final (so the exception is derivable, not lexical, in his model), stress is attracted to diphthongs, and a residue of final-stress roots is 'phonemic'. Merina (standard) dialect explicitly (pp.2, 5, 108).
new_statements.rule_in_words: Default: primary stress on the penult (right-to-left trochaic pattern enforced by *Clash, *Lapse and NonFinality; the rightmost stress is primary, e.g. mandéha 'to go', mahíta 'to see', làndihàzu 'cotton'). Weak roots (the -tra/-ka/-na class, underlyingly consonant-final) get antepenultimate primary stress because their final vowel is epenthetic and post-lexical (p.134-135); nasal-final non-weak roots surface with final stress after post-nasal apocope (p.129); stress is attracted to diphthongs (§3.8.2, p.208: 'stress is attracted to diphthongs in Malagasy'); and a residue of roots carries phonemic final stress, mostly with final [e] (p.211, e.g. lehibé 'big'). Word-level suffixes (imperative -a, etc.) shift stress rightward (§3.6.1).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Secondary stresses fall on alternating syllables leftward from the primary (right-to-left trochaic); Albro argues explicitly (p.123, table (17) bottom row, e.g. mifampiraharàha) against left-to-right secondary footing.
new_statements.exceptions: Weak/pseudo-weak roots (antepenult), nasal-final non-weak roots (final), diphthong attraction (quantity-sensitive, final stress on diphthongs), phonemic final stress (mostly /e/-final, but also vuvú), opaque stress under vowel-hiatus deletion (§3.8.1), stress-bearing prefixes, stress shift under word-level suffixes.
new_statements.identity_note: Albro 2005 describes the Merina dialect explicitly ('the Merina dialect (the standard dialect) of Malagasy', pp.2, 5, 108). Raoniarisoa 1990 is 'a Malagasy dialect' = Merina per Glottolog's note; Rakotofiringa 1982 is Malgache-Merina by title. new_statements.quote: [PDF p.26 = p.14] There is a general agreement among investigators on Malagasy word-accent that it falls on one of the last three syllables in (primary and secondary) stems (Dahle 1877, p38; Dahl 1952, p.153; Verguin (1955, p.522), Rajaona 1972, p.332, Rakotofiringa 1978, p.68; Rafitoson 1980, p.131.). Most of those authors consider the case of proparoxytons ending in <-ka>, <-tra> and <-na> as an exception ... [PDF p.29 = p.17] To sum up, as far as accent placement in Malagasy words is concerned, most authors agree that, as a rule, accent is on either the ultimate, penultimate or antepenultimate syllable in Malagasy words. Thus, accent in Malagasy is not fix but free. By convention, Malagasy accent is represented in the orthography when there is risk of confusion between pairs of words such as, e.g. <tanana> (hand) and <tanàna> (town); <manda> (wall) and <mandà> (to deny).

new_statements.rule_in_words: Merina (the author's native dialect = Official Malagasy base). Surveying and endorsing the descriptive consensus (Dahle 1877, Dahl 1952, Verguin 1955, Rajaona 1972, Rakotofiringa 1978, Rafitoson 1980): word accent falls on one of the last three syllables of (primary and secondary) stems and of derived words; antepenultimate accent is essentially confined to words ending in -ka, -tra, -na, which most authors treat as exceptional/'extrametrical', so that accent is otherwise on one of the last two syllables; within that window accent is 'not fixed but free' and orthography marks it where minimal pairs exist (tanana 'hand' vs tanàna 'town', manda 'wall' vs mandà 'to deny'). Suffixation shifts the accent one syllable rightward (tsínjo -> fitsinjóvana; imperatives mandéha -> mandehána, miláza -> milazà), with listed exceptions (aina -> fiaínana etc.); possessive enclitics -nao, -nay, -ntsika, -nareo attract accent, -ko and -ny do not. The thesis's own theoretical claim (chs.2.4, 6.7) is that syllable prominence is assigned by intonation (the nuclear high tone of the intonation-group falls on the rightmost lexically accented syllable; words not final in an intonation-group may surface with no tonic syllable), that sentence-level accent placement is therefore not predictable from syntax, and that 'lexical accent' is the prominence pattern of words spoken in citation intonation; Malagasy 'is not a tonal language' (p.13).
new_statements.secondary_stress: §2.2.2 (pp.27-28): free morphemes of four or more syllables carry a second accent, typically on the initial syllable (Rakotofiringa 1978, Domenichini-Ramiaramanana 1977 treat it as secondary, Rajemisa-Raolison 1985 as equal); prefixes or prefix strings can carry a second accent; in reduplications and compounds each member keeps its accent, the non-final one being 'subordinate'/secondary for Dahle and Dahl (Dahl 1952: the secondary intensity accent is rhythmic, not phonological); for Rafitoson primary vs secondary is a phrase-level distinction (last accent of an accentual group = primary). The author (§6.7.3, p.252): in polysyllables there may be two 'accented' syllables but only the rightmost bears the high tone; the leftmost 'may have some relevance in rhythm which has not been investigated here'.
new_statements.exceptions: antepenult accent in -ka/-tra/-na words (treated as extrametrical final syllables); suffixal accent shift exceptions aina -> fiainana, fona -> fifonana, tana -> tanana (explained in §2.3.3.1); enclitics -ko, -ny do not take accent while -nao, -nay, -ntsika, -nareo do; loanwords from French and English keep or modify their source accent by etymology, medium, orthography and intonation rather than by a last-three-syllables repair (§2.3-2.4); abbreviations (Ji.Ra.Ma., O.N.U.) take the high tone on a lexically unaccented final syllable; a polysyllable not final in its intonation-group may have no tonic syllable at all (Antananarivo renivohitra) (p.53).
new_statements.identity_note: Raoniarisoa 1990 describes the Merina dialect (province of Antananarivo; the author's native dialect), which she equates for practical purposes with Official Malagasy = the core of plat1254; Betsileo figures only as some listeners' dialect in a perception experiment, not as an object of description. Rakotofiringa's thesis is on 'malgache-merina' (Merina) by its title. Fortin 2007 treats Indonesian, not Malagasy.

tone_statements.quote: Howe concludes that pitch is the primary phonetic cue of voicing, and thus Central Malagasy constitutes a language with lexical tone. ... Malagasy is claimed to have contrastive lexical tone that is correlated with historical voicing (Howe 2017), and this is confirmed in my dataset: when a pitch accented syllable is followed by a syllable with an underlying voiced obstruent, thus lexically specified with a low tone, as in the word azy /'a.zi̥ /, the f0 of the post-tonic syllable does not show a delayed peak of the preceding pitch accent.
tone_statements.summary: Per Howe 2017: high vs low lexical tone on syllables with historically voiceless vs voiced obstruent onsets, others toneless; confirmed in own F0 data; separate post-lexical stress. 3+ toned forms.

sources.quote: 'Malagasy is a stress language. Stress can appear on the final, penultimate, or antepenultimate syllable, and minimal pairs exist (e.g., [ˈla.la.na] “road” and [laˈla.na] “law”) [O'Neill 2015]. However, stress has been argued to be post-lexical [Albro 2005], generally appearing on the penultimate syllable of the underlying form. In the case of words with antepenultimate stress, such as [ˈla.la.na], it is argued that the final vowel is epenthetic and extrametrical [Albro 2005; Raoniarisoa 1990].'

sources.quote: According to Beaujard (1998) and Keenan & Polinsky (1998), main stress in Malagasy is always assigned to one of the last three syllables of a word. Main stress generally falls on the penult, as shown in (8a). However, lexical and morphological factors interfere with this basic stress pattern. Words ending in –tra, -ka, –[ña; garbled '–µ a' in text layer], and -na generally receive main stress on the antepenult. The minimal contrast between (8a) and (8b) shows that the antepenult stress pattern is lexically conditioned. The final syllable can also be stressed in certain lexical and morphological contexts.

sources.note: Secondary survey statement: penult default within a three-syllable right-edge window; -tra/-ka/-ña/-na finals take antepenult stress and this is 'lexically conditioned' (minimal pair tanana/tànana); final stress in some /e/-final roots and by morphology (active/passive milaza/milazà); secondary stress on every second syllable before main stress in words of four or more syllables. sources.quote: 'Malagasy has right-to-left trochaic stress. Primary stress is final in the word. Stress is phonemic in some words and prefixes. Stress is attracted to heavy syllables (syllables are heavy in Malagasy if they contain a long vowel or a diphthong), sometimes causing a stress clash. Lapse may occur due to phonemic stress in prefixes and also due to avoidance of footing final epenthetic vowels.' and 'Post-nasal final vowel deletion: Vowels that would otherwise be unstressed are not pronounced after a nasal, although the stress pattern acts as though the vowel is there.'
